Content:
Let's consider the function [MATH: f(x),] shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/ec9c9120b767fc3336f3fbf6856feb01]

Content:
Note the following:

Content:
- The function is not defined for [MATH: x<0,] nor is it defined for [MATH: x > 2.]
- The function has filled circles at [MATH: x=0] and [MATH: x=2,] so it is defined at both of these points.
- In addition, the function is defined for every value of [MATH: x] between [MATH: 0] and [MATH: 2.]

Content:
Therefore, the domain of this function is

Content:

Content:
We can also express the domain using interval notation:

Content:
[MATH: x\in [0,2]]

Content:
The square brackets [MATH: [\:]] indicate that the endpoints [MATH: x=0] and [MATH: x=2] are included in the domain.

Content:
Consider the function [MATH: f(x)=2x,] shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/02942558f42c999b955e93ecc9211305]

Content:
No matter which number [MATH: x] we pick as an input, [MATH: f(x)] always will return an output. Therefore, we can write the domain of this function as

Content:
[MATH: x\in (-\infty,\infty).]

Content:
Let's compare this to the function [MATH: g(x) = \dfrac 1 x,] shown below:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/526dedd5f7a9472d7ad8c53c0c33dc46]

Content:
We cannot substitute the value [MATH: x=0] into the function [MATH: g(x)] because division by zero is undefined. Therefore, [MATH: x=0] is not part of the domain of [MATH: g(x).] However, we can use any other number [MATH: x] as input for [MATH: g(x).] Therefore, the domain of [MATH: g(x)] is

Content:
[MATH: x\in (-\infty, 0)\cup (0,\infty).]

Content:
This notation means that any number apart from zero can be used as an input for [MATH: g(x).]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The domain of a function is the set of all input values for which it is defined.

Content:

Content:

Item 2 — Example: Determining the Domain of a Function From a Mapping Diagram or Table

| [MATH: f(x)] | [MATH: -2] | [MATH: -2] | [MATH: -1] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 2] |

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The domain is the set of all input values for which the function is defined. In the table, this corresponds to the set of [MATH: x]-values in the first row:

[MATH: \{ -2,-1,0,2,4,6\}]

[IMG: /graphics/eb02e5985a500cac069ebd99109a0ed1]

Content:
Note the following:

Content:
- The function is not defined for [MATH: x<0,] nor is it defined for [MATH: x > 2.]
- The function has open circles at [MATH: x=0] and [MATH: x=2,] so it is not defined at either of these points.
- However, the function is defined for every value of [MATH: x] between [MATH: 0] and [MATH: 2.]

Content:
Therefore, the domain of this function is

Content:
[MATH: 0 \lt x \lt 2,]

Content:
which we can write using interval notation as

Content:
[MATH: x\in (0,2).]

Content:
The parentheses [MATH: (\:)] indicate that the endpoints [MATH: x=0] and [MATH: x=2] are excluded from the domain.

Item 7 — Tutorial: Functions Defined on Semi-Open Intervals

Content:
It's possible for a function to have one endpoint included in the domain and another endpoint excluded.

Content:

Content:
[MATH: -2 \leq x \lt 2,]

Content:
which we can write using interval notation as

Content:

Item 11 — Tutorial: The Domain of a Function Given as a Graph

Content:
Consider the function [MATH: f(x)=2x,] shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/02942558f42c999b955e93ecc9211305]

Content:
No matter which number [MATH: x] we pick as an input, [MATH: f(x)] always will return an output. Therefore, we can write the domain of this function as

Content:
[MATH: x\in (-\infty,\infty).]

Content:
Let's compare this to the function [MATH: g(x) = \dfrac 1 x,] shown below:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/526dedd5f7a9472d7ad8c53c0c33dc46]

Content:
We cannot substitute the value [MATH: x=0] into the function [MATH: g(x)] because division by zero is undefined. Therefore, [MATH: x=0] is not part of the domain of [MATH: g(x).] However, we can use any other number [MATH: x] as input for [MATH: g(x).] Therefore, the domain of [MATH: g(x)] is

Content:
[MATH: x\in (-\infty, 0)\cup (0,\infty).]

Content:
This notation means that any number apart from zero can be used as an input for [MATH: g(x).]
